new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (676 pp., pdftk 2010 output, text layer present). extracted text of PDF p. 15 = printed p. 11, section 'Orthographical decisions', point 3, reads exactly: '[ə] is a prominent feature of Buang phonology, being as it is the open transition between consonants both within words and between words. It could be regarded as neutralisation of the vowels in the unstressed position. It is always unstressed and could be omitted from the orthography, nevertheless, to prevent the sometime appearance in text of long sequences of consonants, and possible confusion with digraphs, it has been. It also gives text a more "normal" appearance. The symbol chosen was e, since in some songs the shewa is sung a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule is stated in any accessible source. Hooley's explicit generalisations are (i) unstressed syllables contain only schwa or a, i.e. any full (non-a) vowel is stressed, and (ii) long vowels are always stressed (Hooley 1962a:10 as reported by Sankoff 1968:94). Position within the word is otherwise lexical: the 2010 dictionary marks stress on every headword and needs an é diacritic to disambiguate stressed e; verbs 'stressed on the first syllable' vs. not form a morphological class (a-/na-/se- allomorphy). Counting the dictionary's 3,871 stress-marked transcriptions: disyllables are 71% final-stressed (a.ˈmaⁿd) vs 29% initial (ˈa.ma); trisyllables 79% penult, 13% final, 9% initial — i.e. stress sits on the (last) full-vowel syllable of the root, with reduced/prefixal initial syllables unstressed, but pairs like aga [ˈa.ᵑɡa] 'cob' vs aġa [a.ˈᵑɢa] 'eat' show it is not predictable from segments alone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the 2010 dictionary transcriptions occasionally carry ˌ on an initial syllable (e.g. ˌa.ʁe.ˈᵐbu), without explanation.
new_statements.exceptions: Sankoff 1968:94-95 notes that in the headwater dialect (her Dialect A) the long-vowel rule is inapplicable (length not phonemic there) and that vowel shifts 'frequently change the stress from syllable to syllable' between dialects and villages; Hooley 2010 notes clitics ba=/be=, ga=/ge=, ma=/me= occur unstressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, dictionary citation forms (Mapos I village speech, Central Buang); the 'ner niweek' (ˈ) mark in the 2010 dictionary is a per-word lexical stress mark.
new_statements.identity_note: Central Buang = Mapos Buang [bzh], mapo1242. The dictionaries describe the speech of Mapos I village (the 'Mapos' dialect; Hooley 1976:341 distinguishes Mapos Buang from the headwater dialect within Central Buang). Sankoff 1968's Dialect B = Mapos/Central Buang, Dialect A = headwater dialect (also mapo1242), Dialect C = Mangga Buang (mang1404, a separate language). Adams & Lauck 1985's stress remarks concern the Mumeng dialect chain (Patep etc.), not this language.

That is the whole of the stress content (a full-text search for stress/accent the txt: 'Stress' x1, 'stress' x1, 'stressed' x1, 'tone' x1 in the heading only); no default position, domain, weight condition or second…
new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the existing statement from the 2010 dictionary (lexical, unpredictable stress with vowel neutralisation in unstressed syllables): the OPD states it more directly ('Stress is phonemic') and supplies the minimal pair the dictionary lacks. It fills the catalog record's empty rule field rather than contradicting it. Scope confirmed on p. 1: 'The data herein applies only to the Central Buang dialect.'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive (phonemic) and its position is not given by any rule; the minimal pair ḳe'le 'tree, wood' (final stress) vs. 'ḳale 'rubbish' (initial stress) shows two disyllables differing only in stress placement. Unstressed syllables neutralise every vowel except /ɑ/ (the neutralised vowel surfaces as the non-phonemic transitional schwa, written <e>, p. 5 'Conventions: Phonological'). No default position, no domain and no weight condition is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The only qualification is that /ɑ/ alone escapes neutralisation in unstressed syllables. Vowel length is separately noted as either a suprasegmental (Hooley 1970) or a phoneme (Kivung 1974) (p. 3), not tied to stress. No tone is described despite the section heading.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD is explicitly restricted to the Central Buang dialect (Mapos Buang, ISO bzh; villages Humek, Mapos I and II, Sëhayo, Wij, Römaröm, Sebulek, Saggee, Seyuwee, Pepeknë), i.e. the catalog's languoid; it does not cover the Headwaters dialect. Data checked by Bruce Hooley, modified January 2014, transcribed by Ryan Pennington.

new_statements.quote: The rules for the occurrence of stress in polysyllabic words are as follows: (1) Long vowels are always stressed. (2) CVC syllables are always stressed. If there are two CVC syllables in a word, the first takes the primary stress and the second a secondary stress. (3) VC and C syllables are never stressed. (4) In words without a long vowel or a CVC syllable, if the last two syllables are open, then the penultimate syllable is stressed. (5) Occurrence of an additional syllable due to affixation does not change the stress on a word.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog records Central Buang as 'lexical' on the strength of Hooley 1992 OPD ('Stress is phonemic', ḳe'le 'tree' vs 'ḳale 'rubbish') and the 2010 dictionary intro. The 1970 dissertation, the same author's full phonology, instead gives explicit predictable rules: stress is assigned by syllable weight (long vowel / closed syllable) with penultimate default, and schwa is a non-phonemic open transition that is never stressed. The two are alternative analyses of the same facts (1970: schwa non-phonemic, so /k.le/ = C+CV -> final full syllable stressed, /kale/ = CV.CV -> penult; 1992: schwa-vs-full-vowel contrast reinterpreted as phonemic stress with vowel neutralization in unstressed syllables)…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The phonological word has exactly one (primary) stressed syllable, with up to four unstressed syllables before it and one or two after (p. 108-109). Placement is predictable from syllable shape: a long (geminate) vowel or a closed CVC syllable takes the stress; C syllables (whose peak is the non-phonemic schwa 'open transition') and VC syllables are never stressed; in words made only of open short syllables the penultimate is stressed. Non-final unstressed CV syllables contain only /a/ (p. 112-113, 116); word-initial V /a/ is stressed before a short open syllable but unstressed before a closed or long syllable ('ama 'his father' vs a'mam 'your father', p. 111-112). Affixal syllables do not shift stress. The alternative presentation (sec. 5.6, pp. 122-123) restates the same rules: geminate-vowel syllables always stressed, VC never, other closed syllables always (first primary, second secondary), any syllable with schwa peak unstressed, otherwise penultimate. Phrase stress falls on the normally stressed syllable of the final word of the phonological phrase (p. 106). Intonation contours are described (5.1); no lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Where a word has two CVC (closed) syllables the first carries primary and the second secondary stress (pp. 113, 115, 122); in compounds the would-be word stresses are not equal, one being reduced to secondary stress, which is a reason to treat compounds as words (p. 140).
new_statements.exceptions: V-only clitics (deictic, question marker a, vocative o) are outside the phonological word and unstressed (fn. p. 111); the verbal suffix -in (the only VC syllable inside polysyllables) is never stressed (p. 112); only one non-compound CVCV word with a non-/a/ first vowel was found (l8v6 'to go downstream', p. 116); Class I verbs split into those stressed on the first syllable vs those with unstressed /a/-initial syllable (ch. 6, pp. ~ 9385ff of text).
new_statements.identity_note: The dissertation describes Mapos Buang, 'the language spoken in and around the village of Mapos in the Morobe District' (Intro, text l. 1741), i.e. the central dialect of the Buang/Mumeng dialect chain (Mapos, Wagau) = Glottolog mapo1242 Central Buang/Mapos Buang; the headwater dialect (Manga) and Kapin are treated as separate languages/dialects and occasionally cited for contrast (e.g. final /y/, p. 115-116).

readall_conflicts: Hooley 1970 (PhD, ch. 5, pp. 114-115 and 122-123) states that word stress in Mapos Buang is predictable: long vowels and closed (CVC) syllables are always stressed, C (schwa-peak) and VC syllables never, otherwise the penultimate of open syllables, with primary on the first and secondary on the second of two closed syllables. Hooley 1992 (OPD, p. 4) and Hooley & Rambok 2010 (dictionary intro, p. 11) instead say 'Stress is phonemic' and treat schwa as the neutralization of vowels in unstressed position. The disagreement is analytic rather than factual: in 1970 schwa is a non-phonemic open transition and stress follows from syllable structure; in 1992/2010 the schwa/full-vowel distribution is reclassified as contrastive stress plus reduction (minimal pair ḳe'le 'tree' vs 'ḳale 'rubbish' = 1970 /k.le/ C+CV vs /kale/ CV.CV). The catalog's 'lexical' entry follows the later, briefer sources; the fullest description (1970) supports a weight-sensitive, right-edge (penult-default) system.
